lenses.sp: Wants a large, steady, cheap company with a strong balance sheet.
lenses.vd: In Benjamin Graham's spirit: a great business, but this lens's own price test fails.

ch.r: Market value above ₹5,000 crore
ch.w: Graham avoided small companies; ₹5,000 crore is our Indian translation of 'adequate size'.

ch.r: Current assets ÷ current liabilities ≥ 2
ch.w: For every ₹100 it owes within a year, it holds ₹340 of cash, stock and dues coming in.

ch.r: Long-term debt ≤ current assets − current liabilities
ch.v: Long-term debt ₹324 cr vs working capital ₹1,700 cr
ch.w: Graham wanted the short-term cushion alone to be able to repay long-term loans.

ch.n: A profit every year for 10 years
ch.r: Positive earnings in each of the last 10 years
ch.v: Profit in all 4 yrs we have
ch.w: No loss in the years we can see; the earlier years are not in the free data.

ch.r: Dividends every year for 20 years (India: 10 years)
ch.w: 10 dividends in 10 years with no gap longer than 18 months.

ch.n: Earnings per share up a third in 10 years
ch.r: EPS +33% over 10 years (3-year averages at each end)
ch.w: EPS (average of the first 2 vs last 2 years we have) moved +29%.

ch.r: PE ≤ 15 on 3-year average earnings
ch.w: You pay ₹23 for every ₹1 of average yearly profit over the last 3 yrs.
You pay ₹5.22 for every ₹1 of net worth.

ch.r: Price < √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share)
ch.w: With EPS ₹78.9 and book value ₹279 per share, Graham's ceiling price is ₹703.

lenses.st: Wonderful business at a fair price
lenses.sp: Wants a simple business with a lasting edge, high returns without debt, and trustworthy managers.
lenses.vd: In Warren Buffett's spirit: a great business, and the price passes both this lens's own price test and the fair-value check (₹1,454 vs fair value ₹2,050).

ch.r: Could you explain how it makes money in two sentences?
q: What does it sell, and to whom?
Will people still need this in 10 years?

ch.r: A lasting edge: brand, low cost, network or switching costs
q: Why can't a well-funded rival copy it?
Has it kept high returns through bad years?

ch.r: ROE ≥ 15% in at least 8 of the last 10 years, with debt-to-equity < 0.5
ch.w: Strong in 4 of the 4 yrs we can see.

ch.r: No loss in 10 years
ch.w: No loss in the years we can see.

ch.n: Doesn't eat its cash in capex
ch.r: Capex < 50% of operating cash flow (5-year sum)
ch.v: Capex was 16% of cash from operations over 4 yrs
ch.w: Of every ₹100 of cash the business brought in, ₹16 went back into plant and equipment.

ch.r: Share count up no more than 5% over the years we have
ch.w: Your slice of the company hasn't been shrunk by new share issues.

ch.r: Candid, sensible with capital, no governance red flags
ch.v: No management red flags in our automatic checks (checked: auditor changes, CFO/KMP changes, credit ratings, SEBI orders, promoter holding, pledge).
ch.w: Our automatic checks are a starting point only.
q: Do they admit mistakes in the annual report letter?
Have past acquisitions and capex paid off?

ch.n: Bought with a margin of safety
ch.r: Price ≥ 25% below estimated intrinsic value
ch.w: Needs the fair-value (DCF) estimate, which arrives in Stage 4.

lenses.st: Great business at a fair price; invert
lenses.sp: Prefers a great business at a fair price, and first asks how the investment could fail.
lenses.vd: In Charlie Munger's spirit: a great business, and the price passes both this lens's own price test and the fair-value check (₹1,454 vs fair value ₹2,050).

ch.r: Average ROCE ≥ 20% over 5 years
ch.w: For every ₹100 in the business it earned about ₹35 a year.

ch.r: PEG (PE ÷ EPS growth) below 2
ch.w: PE 18.4 against EPS growth of 15.3% a year.

ch.r: Promoters own ≥ 25% and have pledged none
ch.w: Owners with lots of their own money in the shares, unborrowed against, tend to act like you would.

ch.n: Invert: how could this go wrong?
ch.r: List the ways you could lose money before the reasons to buy
ch.v: Our checks found no warning signs to start the list with.
q: What would make profits halve?
What would a short-seller say?

ch.r: Only invest in what you truly understand
q: Could you explain this business to a 12-year-old in 2 minutes?

ch.r: PEG < 1 attractive, ~1 fair, ≥ 2 expensive
ch.w: PE 18.4 divided by EPS growth 15.3% a year (growth measured over 3 yrs).

ch.r: Debt-to-equity below 0.35

ch.r: EPS growth 20–25% a year

ch.n: Not a hot stock in a hot industry

story.what_it_does: eClerx is a services company that runs data, analytics, automation and operations work for clients, with delivery teams of about 23,000 people. Its clients include banks and financial firms, fashion and luxury brands, and retailers. It earns most of its revenue in US dollars, and the top ten clients make up about 60% of revenue.
story.plans: Management aims for revenue growth in the top quartile versus peers and an operating EBITDA margin of 24% to 28% for FY27. It plans to win agentic AI deals, return the BFSI business to growth, and spend a similar amount on capex in the second half as in the first. It also proposed a 1:1 bonus issue and a dividend of INR 1.
story.moat: The notes show long-running client relationships and 13 straight quarters of sequential dollar revenue growth. They also show a growing analytics and automation book of about USD 90 million. However, the notes also mention rising pricing pressure, and the top ten clients make up 60% of revenue, so any edge looks modest and not clearly proven.

scenarios.story: Deals convert, BFSI recovers and luxury rebounds, so growth returns to the top quartile while margins stay in the 24-28% band. Agentic AI wins add revenue faster than any price deflation takes away.
signals_to_watch: BFSI growth turnaround, which management moved from Q3 to Q4 FY27
Quarterly deal wins recovering from USD 31 million in Q2 FY27 and ACV holding at last year's level

scenarios.story: Revenue keeps growing sequentially but more slowly, as clients stay selective and decisions take longer. Operating EBITDA margin stays near the low end of the 24-28% range after hiring and wage costs.
signals_to_watch: Operating EBITDA margin staying at or above 24% (Q2 FY27: 23.9%)

scenarios.story: Smaller AI pilot deals, price deflation and softer BFSI, M&D and retail spending push growth down further, while headcount keeps rising faster than revenue. Profit growth lags revenue growth and relies more on volatile currency-driven other income.
signals_to_watch: Dollar revenue growth slowing further from 10.6% year on year in Q2 FY27
Top-10 client concentration (60%) and regulation hitting top-5 and BFSI revenue
